newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai's 31-day shopping spree ends in record sales.
newsitem.headline: Dubai's 31-day shopping spree ends in record sales.

text.p: Dubai's month-long shopping festival generated record sales and boosted the emirate's image as the Gulf's trade and tourism centre, officials said on Sunday.

The glitzy promotional blitz, with daily fireworks displays and a grand fireworks finale on Saturday, lured about two million shoppers from around the world and generated turnover of $1 billion according to initial estimates, they told Reuters.
"Gold did tremendously well, followed by electronics, textiles and carpets," one festival official said.

Dubai's first shop-until-you-drop festival in 1996 attracted 1.5 million people from neighbouring Gulf Arab states, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent and former Soviet republics who spent $800 million.
"Dubai has become a truly international multi-faceted city," Mohammad Alabbar, head of Dubai's economic development department, told a ceremony marking the end of the fiesta.
"Dubai is not only the commercial hub of the Middle East but has firmly established its place on the world tourism and cultural map as a shopping and leisure destination," he said.

Alabbar promised next year's shopping festival, set to open on March 19, would be "bigger, better and much brighter". In addition to the fireworks, five million coloured bulbs lit Dubai's streets, buildings and palm trees during this year's shopping spree.
Dubai, one of seven emirates that make up the UAE, has in recent years stepped up efforts to diversify its economy by promoting trade, industry, tourism and services.
Officials want tourism revenue to match oil income by the year 2000. Tourism accounts for about 11 percent of the emirate's gross domestic product.
The festival was held amid much hype and hoopla with rich raffle prizes including over 130 Japanese cars and 41 kg (90 lb) of gold. Stores offered discounts of between 20 and 70 percent.

A Filipino of Dubai became a "Lexus millionaire" after winning seven cars in a bonanza raffle at the end of the festival which included bazaars, art exhibits, sports events and international dance and theatre troupes.

Dubai's gold committee, which ran a parallel "Dubai city of gold" promotion to help the desert emirate's ambition to replace Singapore as the world's largest distributor of gold, reported brisk sales, especially in the last few days of the promotion.
"We believe gold was the number one attraction of the festival," a committee member told Reuters.
The city's 260 gold retailers reported an increase of up to 70 percent in sales over the last month.
Eight tonnes of gold were sold during the festival for some 320 million dirhams ($87 million), according to official estimates.
